prime.problem: Without a way to count how work grows, you can't tell an O(n) loop from an O(n²) one until it times out, and you can't justify why list.append is cheap even though some appends copy the whole list.
prime.fits: The first card of the course, with no prerequisites. Every later card states a Time O(…) line; this card is where those words, and the amortized argument used by the monotonic stack, deque and two-pointer cards, are defined.
expect: O, Θ, amortized and expected bounds
the doubling array and its geometric series
why growing by a constant is O(n²)
RandomizedCollection: list + dict of index sets, swap with last
prime.goal: Explain why doubling makes append O(1) amortized, tell amortized from expected, and build a multiset with O(1) insert, remove and weighted random pick.

attend: In the 16-append picture, which appends pay extra, and why does the total stay under 3n?
What exactly goes wrong if the list grows by a fixed amount instead of by a factor?
How is amortized O(1) different from expected O(1), and which one does a dict lookup give you?
Why does RandomizedCollection move the last item into the hole instead of deleting from the middle?
Why must add run before discard when the removed copy is already the last item?

must: The buffer doubles when full → copies are 1 + 2 + 4 + … < 2n → total work < 3n for n appends → each append is O(1) amortized, even though a single append can copy everything
Growing by a constant amount → copies are 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) ≈ n²/2 → O(n) amortized per append → 499,999,500,000 copies at n = 10⁶ versus 1,048,575 for doubling

Random pick needs a dense array (one random index) → removal from the middle would shift O(n) items → move the last item into the hole and pop the end → a dict from value to its set of positions keeps every index findable → insert, remove and pick all O(1)

Amortized bounds the total over any sequence (no randomness), expected averages over random choices (hashes, pivots) → a dict is O(1) expected and can degrade to O(n) with colliding keys, while append's bound holds for every sequence
elevated: CPython grows lists by about 1.125×, not 2× → still a constant factor above 1 → the geometric bound still holds, with more frequent but smaller resizes (86 in 10⁶ appends)
The dict stores a set of positions per value → duplicates each keep their own index → a dict of a single index would leave a stale position when one of two equal values is removed
reference: the growth table's step counts (9,966 and 19,931,569 for n log n)

compress.prompt: From memory, write 3–4 sentences explaining why appending to a Python list is O(1) amortized, then sketch the three structures (list, dict of index sets) after insert(1), insert(1), insert(2), remove(1).
checklist: the buffer grows by a constant factor, so the copies form a geometric series below 2n
total cost under 3n, so O(1) per append on average over the sequence, with rare expensive steps
growing by a constant amount would make it O(n²) in total
RandomizedCollection: list for O(1) random pick, dict value → set of indices, swap-with-last removal
amortized ≠ expected: one is over sequences, the other over random choices

retrieve.q: Explain why the card calls list.append O(1) even though append 9 in the picture copies 8 items.
answer: amortized cost = total over the sequence ÷ its length
doubling makes the copies 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 for 16 appends, under 2n
total 31 for 16 appends, about 1.94 each, and always under 3 per append

retrieve.q: Walk through remove(1) on vals = [1, 1, 2] with idx = {1: {0, 1}, 2: {2}}, assuming the set hands back position 0. What moves where, and what are both structures after?
answer: pop position 0 from idx[1]
last = vals[-1] = 2 moves into slot 0
idx[2] gains 0, then loses 2 (the old last index)
vals.pop() drops the end: vals = [2, 1], idx = {1: {1}, 2: {0}}

retrieve.q: A latency-sensitive loop appends to a list and occasionally stalls. Why does the amortized O(1) guarantee not help, and what are two fixes from the card?
answer: amortized bounds the total, not the single worst call; one append can copy the whole list
preallocate the list ([None] * n)
use collections.deque, whose fixed 64-slot blocks never copy everything at once

retrieve.q: Why does a Counter of values fail the RandomizedCollection spec, even though its insert and remove are O(1)?
answer: getRandom must pick proportionally to counts
with only counts, a weighted pick walks the counts: O(number of distinct values)
the list of copies makes the weighting free: one random index

compare.q: RandomizedCollection and Random Pick with Blacklist both keep a dense range to draw from. What does each move into a hole, when does it happen, and how does each fail if you forget to update the dict?
answer: RandomizedCollection moves the last list item into the removed slot, at every remove
the blacklist card maps each banned value below m to an allowed value at or above m, once in the constructor
both give one random call per pick over a dense range
forgetting the index update leaves a stale position (collection) or an unmapped hole that returns a banned value (blacklist)

compare.q: Both this card's list append and the monotonic stack are called amortized O(1). What is being charged in each argument, and why can one step still be expensive?
answer: append: copies are charged to the doubling steps, a geometric series under 2n
monotonic stack: each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so all pops total ≤ n
one append can copy everything; one push can pop many indices
both are bounds on the sequence, not on a single call

predict.q: Suppose CPython grew lists by 1.5× instead of 2×. For 1,000 appends starting at capacity 1, will the total number of copied items be larger or smaller than with doubling, and will append still be O(1) amortized?
predict.answer: Larger: counting with a capacity rounded up at each resize gives 2,120 copies at 1.5× against 1,023 with doubling, because resizes happen more often. It is still O(1) amortized: any constant factor above 1 keeps the copies a geometric series, bounded by a constant times n. Only growing by a fixed amount (499,500 copies here) breaks the bound.

apply.task: Write a 10-line counter that simulates appends into a buffer starting at capacity 1 and returns the total items copied for a given growth factor. Run it for n = 1,000 with factors 2 and 1.5 (round the new capacity up), and with growth by +1. Then explain the three numbers in one sentence each.
apply.done: Your counter prints 1,023 copies for ×2, 2,120 for ×1.5 and 499,500 for +1 (that is 1 + 2 + … + 999), and you can say which two are O(n) and which is O(n²).
apply.hint: Copy cap items whenever size exceeds cap, then set cap = max(cap + 1, ceil(cap × f)).
